overview: Berkeley Group is a premium UK residential developer specialising in large-scale brownfield regeneration, building mixed-use neighbourhoods primarily in London, the South East and Birmingham. The company acquires complex, underused urban land (former gasworks, industrial sites, utility land), secures planning consent and delivers tenure-blind communities of private, affordable and rented homes over multi-year, often decade-long, build-outs. Celebrating its 50th anniversary in FY2026 (year end 30 April), Berkeley is now extending its model into Build to Rent (Berkeley Living) alongside its traditional for-sale housebuilding.

business_model.summary: Berkeley buys brownfield land at the right point in the cycle, invests patient upfront capital in masterplanning, infrastructure and placemaking, then monetises each site over many years through phased for-sale private housing, affordable housing (largely pre-sold/subsidised under Section 106 agreements), commercial space, and increasingly retained Build to Rent (BTR) units. Revenue is project/completion-based rather than recurring: income is recognised on legal completion of homes, so results are lumpy and tied to the phasing of large regeneration schemes (30 long-term sites, 24 in delivery as of FY2026). Forward sales under exchanged contracts (cash due on forward sales was £1,006m at 30 April 2026) provide a degree of revenue visibility 1-3 years out. BTR (Berkeley Living) is building a recurring rental income stream to diversify away from pure trading profit.

revenue_streams.name: Commercial and community space within mixed-use schemes
Build to Rent (Berkeley Living) rental income
Joint ventures (e.g. St Edward, National Grid JV sites)

business_model.customer_type: B2C owner-occupiers and investors, plus B2B/B2G sales to institutional investors, retirement living operators and affordable housing providers (housing associations, local authorities)
business_model.geographic_mix: Concentrated in London (over 70% of homes) and the wider South East/Thames Valley, with an expanding presence in Birmingham; no material international operations

main_competitors: Local/boutique London developers (e.g. Ballymore, Mount Anvil)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest single contributor to new private and affordable homes in London (c.10% of all London homes delivered over the last five years); the only large-scale UK homebuilder whose strategy is built entirely around complex brownfield regeneration rather than greenfield/volume housebuilding. Holds the most valuable land pipeline of any UK housebuilder (reported c.£32bn) even though its plot count is lower than mass-market peers, reflecting high-value London/SE land.

moat_factors.factor: Brownfield land bank and planning expertise
moat_factors.description: Decades of experience navigating complex, contaminated or constrained urban sites, Section 106 negotiations, and relationships with local authorities give Berkeley a pipeline (c.52,700 plots, £6.4bn future gross margin) that is very difficult for new entrants or mass-market peers to replicate

Industry-leading NPS (+77.9 vs industry average +61.4) and build-quality scores (91% of homes with zero/fewer than five defects vs 31% industry average) support premium pricing and support sales velocity in a soft market
Sole large-scale alignment with the Government's brownfield-first agenda gives some preferential positioning in planning policy debates, though this cuts both ways as a lobbying dependency
Net cash (£363m at FY2026) plus £1.4bn of committed facilities post year-end gives Berkeley the ability to hold land through down-cycles rather than being a forced seller, unlike more leveraged peers
Long (8-10+ year) regeneration programmes create switching-cost-like lock-in with local authorities and JV partners, but also tie up capital and slow responsiveness

weaknesses: Heavy geographic concentration in London/SE makes earnings highly sensitive to local demand, affordability and the one regional housing market globally exposed to international buyer sentiment, SDLT surcharges and visa/immigration policy
Long planning and construction lead times (now 8+ years for an apartment building, versus 5 years a decade ago) slow the ability to flex production to short-term demand changes
Premium, higher-value product is more exposed to mortgage rate and affordability shocks than mass-market volume builders
Reliance on Section 106/affordable housing obligations and local authority negotiation creates project-specific delivery and viability risk

growth_drivers: Berkeley 2035 long-term strategy: ~£7bn of free cash flow identified for deployment over 10 years (~£2.5bn land investment, £2bn minimum shareholder returns, £1.2bn Build to Rent platform construction, £1.3bn flexible allocation)

Build to Rent expansion (Berkeley Living) - diversifying into a recurring rental income stream from the existing brownfield pipeline, with assets already transferring from inventory to the BTR investment property platform

Replanning and enhancement of existing land holdings to increase density/value (e.g. Southall/Green Quarter masterplan increased to over 8,000 homes; Woodberry Down enhanced masterplan increased to 6,500 homes) rather than acquiring new land, improving margins without new capital at risk

Structural undersupply in London and the South East (London delivering under 10% of its MHCLG annual new homes target; South East shortfall of c.33,000 homes/46% per year) implies a large multi-year demand backlog once market conditions and policy normalise
Advocacy for Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) reform and streamlined planning/Building Safety Regulator processes, which, if enacted, would be a material catalyst for volumes and viability

Continued cadence of share buybacks when the share price trades below NAV per share (£233m returned in FY2026; further £640m targeted in returns by 30 September 2030), supporting per-share value even without volume growth
Long-term London fundamentals (global financial centre status, international demand, heritage/security appeal) expected to underpin values over the cycle

business.description: Cash due on forward sales fell from £1,403m (FY2025) to £1,006m (FY2026), reflecting subdued market urgency; a weak London sales market directly reduces near-term profit visibility

business.risk: Long planning and build-out cycle risk
business.description: Management states it now takes at least eight years to complete an apartment building in London from acquisition through planning, Section 106, consultation and construction (versus five years a decade ago), with no certainty of final consent even after a decade of engagement (e.g. Peckham Rye scheme refused after 10 years)

Pipeline has declined from ~12,000 to ~11,000 plots year on year; delivery depends on securing planning consents, Building Safety Regulator (Gateway 2/3) approvals, and local authority cooperation across 30 complex regeneration sites
Identified as a principal risk; defects, safety incidents or build-quality lapses could damage the premium brand that underpins pricing power

financial.description: Pre-tax profit has declined for three consecutive years (FY2023 £604.0m, FY2024 £557.3m, FY2025 £528.9m, FY2026 £451.4m) and pre-tax ROE has fallen from 18.7% (FY2023) to 12.5% (FY2026)

Listed as a principal risk; while net cash (£363m) and £1.4bn of facilities (post year-end) are currently healthy, large, long-dated regeneration schemes require sustained access to funding through market cycles, and Green Bond/Green Term Loan covenants tie capital to specific uses
Commitment to £1.2bn of BTR platform investment plus ongoing land investment and shareholder returns within a ~£7bn 10-year envelope leaves limited flexibility if cash generation disappoints

regulatory.description: UK Government's Building Safety Levy (expected to raise ~£3.4bn over 10 years from developers, rate linked to local house prices with a 50% brownfield discount) is now due to take effect from autumn 2026, directly increasing development costs; Berkeley has publicly lobbied for it to be scrapped

Creditors include £226.3m of provisions for post-completion development obligations including building fire-safety matters; ongoing Building Safety Act compliance (Gateway 2/3 regulator approvals) adds cost and time to high-rise schemes

Identified as top principal risks ("Political outlook" and "Regulation and reporting"); Section 106 affordable housing requirements, Residential Property Developer Tax (RPDT, 29% on developer profits), CIL, and SDLT surcharges all directly affect project viability and are called out by management as needing reform
Affordability regulation and mortgage guarantee scheme limits affect first-time buyer and investor demand for completed homes

macro.risk: UK interest rates and mortgage affordability
macro.description: Higher-for-longer UK rates directly affect buyer affordability and investor appetite in Berkeley's premium London/SE market, and the FY2026 statement notes continued market caution from economic uncertainty and political change

A decade of SDLT increases and surcharges introduced since rates were near zero has curtailed early-stage investment in new homes; London is also exposed to shifts in international buyer sentiment and visa/immigration policy
Principal risk category "Cost and availability of materials and labour"; construction cost inflation compresses margins on fixed-price-sold forward contracts
New-build housing is a highly cyclical, capital-intensive sector; national starts fell to record lows (~7,500 in the last year per management, despite a Q1 2026 uptick)

macro_factors.industry_outlook: UK (and particularly London/South East) new-build housing remains structurally undersupplied against government targets, but near-term activity is subdued: London is delivering under 10% of its MHCLG annual target, and the South East has an estimated annual shortfall of c.33,000 homes (46% below need). Management argues policy reform (SDLT cuts, Building Safety Levy removal/sunset, faster Building Safety Regulator processing) is required to unlock supply; absent reform, volumes are likely to stay depressed into FY2027
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - premium housebuilding/regeneration is a long-cycle, capital-intensive, discretionary-purchase business; Berkeley's own profit has fallen for three straight years (FY2023-FY2026) reflecting the current down-cycle
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - directly affects mortgage affordability for buyers, investor yields for BTR/institutional sales, and Berkeley's own cost of debt/return on cash deposits (net finance income fell to £1.6m in FY2026 from £14.2m in FY2025 due to rate moves and lower deposit balances)

recent_developments.event: UK Building Safety Levy due to take effect autumn 2026 (~£3.4bn to be raised from developers over 10 years, house-price-linked rate with 50% brownfield discount); Berkeley has publicly called for it to be scrapped

Trading update (May-August 2026 period) at AGM: continued market caution from economic uncertainty and political change; profit expected weighted to H1 FY2027; £60m returned to shareholders via buybacks in the first four months; net cash guided to ~£250m at half year; company remains ahead of run-rate for its 2030 shareholder return target; renewed call for SDLT reform

FY2026 annual results (year to 30 April 2026): pre-tax profit £451.4m (down from £528.9m), net cash £363.3m (up £26.0m) after £233.0m of share buybacks, NAV per share up 9% to £39.17, pre-tax ROE 12.5% (down from 14.9%); cash due on forward sales fell to £1,006m from £1,403m; guidance reiterated for a similar level of profit in FY2027 and a ~£300m net cash target; banking facilities extended post year-end to £1.4bn
Leadership transition: Rob Perrins moved from CEO to Executive Chair; Richard Stearn (CFO since 2015) became Chief Executive; long-serving Chairman Michael Dobson stepped down at the AGM

Berkeley 2035 ten-year strategy announced, including the Berkeley Living Build to Rent platform and a ~£7bn ten-year free cash flow allocation framework (land investment, shareholder returns, BTR construction, flexible capital)

Planning progress on key regeneration sites: enhanced masterplan at The Green Quarter/Southall approved (now 8,000+ homes) and at Woodberry Down (now 6,500 homes); first Berkeley Living (BTR) homes launched at Alexandra Gate and Kidbrooke Village; two BTR assets transferred from inventory into the investment property platform

Analyst consensus rated 'Moderate Buy' with average price target materially above the prevailing share price (consensus targets reported in the ~4,400p region versus the stock trading around 3,150-3,950p through 2026), reflecting a market that has derated the shares faster than earnings have fallen amid UK housing demand concerns

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Results (23 June 2026) and AGM Trading Statement (11 September 2026)

items.notes: Part of the rolling four-year ~£1.4bn cumulative pre-tax profit plan; September 2026 update confirmed trading operating within this plan, with profit weighted towards H1 FY2027
Reflects ongoing shareholder returns, BTR investment and land acquisition activity; future cash flow improvements expected from reduced new phase commitments and paused land investment

items.target: Further £640m of returns (dividends and/or buybacks) by 30 September 2030
items.notes: Company stated it is running ahead of the run-rate needed to hit this target; £60m returned via buybacks in the first four months of FY2027

items.target: ~£7bn: ~£2.5bn land investment, ~£2.0bn minimum shareholder returns, ~£1.2bn Build to Rent platform, ~£1.3bn flexible allocation
items.notes: Long-term capital allocation framework rather than annual guidance; land investment is being achieved largely through replanning/enhancing existing holdings rather than new site acquisition in the current environment

guidance.management_commentary: Executive Chair Rob Perrins said FY2026 performance was in line with guidance and reflected disciplined cost control and agile response to a challenging macro and regulatory backdrop. Management reiterated that the business prioritises financial strength over annual profit targets, and continues to call for Stamp Duty Land Tax reform, scrapping of the Building Safety Levy, a sunset clause on the Residential Property Developer Tax, and operational fixes at the Building Safety Regulator, arguing these changes would be fiscally neutral or better for the Exchequer due to higher transactional and corporation tax receipts from increased housebuilding activity.

bull_case: Structurally undersupplied London/South East market (London delivering under 10% of its housing target) implies a large pent-up demand backlog that Berkeley, as the dominant brownfield regeneration specialist, is best placed to capture once rates/policy normalise

Strong balance sheet (net cash of £363m plus £1.4bn of facilities) gives Berkeley the flexibility to keep buying back stock below NAV, hold land through the downturn rather than being a forced seller, and fund the new BTR platform without needing new equity

Clear, disciplined 10-year capital allocation framework (Berkeley 2035, ~£7bn of free cash flow) with a concrete 2030 shareholder return commitment (further £640m) gives investors visibility and a self-help source of per-share value even if volumes stay depressed

Industry-leading quality and customer satisfaction metrics (NPS +77.9 vs +61.4 industry average, 91% of homes with minimal defects) support premium pricing and sales velocity relative to mass-market peers

Build to Rent (Berkeley Living) diversifies the business into a more recurring, lower-volatility income stream, monetising the existing land bank differently and reducing pure dependence on the for-sale cycle
bear_case: Three consecutive years of declining pre-tax profit (£604m → £557m → £529m → £451m) and falling ROE (18.7% → 12.5%) show the current down-cycle is deep and forward sales cover (down from £1.4bn to £1.0bn) is shrinking, with no clear near-term catalyst for reacceleration

Incoming UK Building Safety Levy (from autumn 2026) and existing Residential Property Developer Tax add further cost burden precisely as volumes are weak, and management's lobbying for reform may not succeed, leaving structurally higher costs permanently embedded

Extremely long and lengthening planning/consent timelines (now 8+ years for an apartment scheme) and outright planning refusals even after a decade of engagement (Peckham Rye) create real execution risk on a pipeline with limited substitutability

Heavy concentration in London/SE residential leaves Berkeley highly exposed to a single regional market's affordability, interest-rate and international-buyer dynamics, with limited geographic diversification to offset a prolonged London downturn

New Build to Rent platform (Berkeley Living) is unproven at scale, requires significant capital (£1.2bn planned) and dilutes the company's historically simple trading-profit model with real-estate-style valuation and operating risk under a new, recently appointed CEO
